To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the analytical formalism of perturbative QCD is very successful in describing the hadronic final states in high-energy collisions, in particular in describing the multiplicity distributions and inclusive spectra of particles with momenta below 10 GeV/c.

(i) the MLLA formalism is able to describe a variety of hadronic observables, in particular the inclusive particle spectra, with a precision of about 20%; (ii) the MLLAA is a useful tool to study the evolution of the parton density in a hadron, and (iii) the MLLLA is able to predict the multiplicity and the inclusive particle spectra for a wide range of particle energies, from the TeV to the GeV region

(a) analytical calculations in QCD can be performed at next-to-leading logarithm accuracy (b) they reproduce data on multiparticle production at the level of the leading logarithm (c) they are not able to describe the data at higher order (d) the leading logarithm approximation is a very good approximation to the data.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following issues: 1) Theoretical aspects of the analytical formalism: the derivation of the MLLA equations, their solution, their extension to the case of non-vanishing masses, the role of the renormalization and factorization schemes.
the following topics: (a) Analytical QCD and the multiplicity problem.
the following questions: 1. What is the role of the QCD scale in hadron production processes?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
perturbative QCD can be applied to a large variety of observables in hadronic collisions, even for very small momentum transfers.
the perturbative QCD approach, based on the factorization theorem and the DGLAP equations, is able to describe the bulk of hadron production at high energy in a satisfactory manner.
the analytical approach is a useful tool to describe hadron production at low pT. It is a good approximation at high energy and large multiplicities, where the perturbative regime is reached.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
analytical QCD is an excellent tool for the description of the soft and semi-hard hadronic final state in hard collision processes.
the MLLA is able to describe the gross features of multiparticle production, while it fails for the detailed structure of the spectra.
analytical calculations are able to describe the main features of the experimental data, provided the cut-off is chosen appropriately.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the perturbative QCD picture of multiparticle production is not limited to hard processes, but it can be applied to a wide range of observables.
the perturbative formalism is able to provide a good description of hadronic observables, even at low transverse momenta, and that this success is not limited to high multiplicity events.
the analytical approach provides a useful framework to understand hadronic final states, and that this framework can be extended to the next-to-MLLA level.
